title: Java Delete Files
learningObjectives: Delete a file with File.delete and inspect its boolean result.
Use Files.delete for explicit failure reporting.
Use Files.deleteIfExists when absence is acceptable.
Distinguish deleting files from deleting non-empty directories.
Apply safe path checks and avoid deleting unintended data.

understand.concept: Java supports deletion through File.delete and the NIO Files API. File.delete returns a boolean, which can make failure reasons difficult to diagnose. Files.delete throws IOException when deletion fails and NoSuchFileException when the path is absent. Files.deleteIfExists returns false if nothing existed to delete. A directory can normally be deleted only when it is empty; always validate the target path before destructive operations.
understand.whyItMatters: Deletion is a destructive file-system operation. Correct API selection and careful target validation help prevent accidental data loss, while explicit exception handling lets applications distinguish an absent file from a failed deletion.
understand.analogy: Think of a path as a labeled address to a storage location; the address and the data stored there are different things.
understand.analogyLimit: A path is not a guarantee that the target exists or that the program has permission to access it.

explain.narrative:
## Delete a file with the NIO API

Use `Files.delete(path)` when the target is expected to exist. It throws an `IOException` if deletion fails and a `NoSuchFileException` if the path is absent. Use `Files.deleteIfExists(path)` when an already-absent target is an acceptable outcome; it returns `false` when there was nothing to delete and `true` when the path was removed.

The older `File.delete()` method returns a boolean. A false result indicates that deletion did not happen, but it provides less detail about the reason.

## Directories and non-empty folders

A directory can normally be deleted only when it is empty. Deleting a directory is not the same as recursively deleting its contents. Recursive deletion requires walking the tree and handling failures at each entry; it should never be added casually.

## Validate the target before deletion

Confirm that the path is inside the application-owned directory and matches the exact file the user intended to remove. Do not trust raw user-supplied path strings. Resolve and normalize paths, check that the resolved target remains under the approved base directory, and consider symbolic links and race conditions. An existence check alone does not guarantee that a later delete will succeed.

## Handle failures explicitly

Deletion can fail because the path is absent, access is denied, the target is a non-empty directory, or the file system reports another I/O error. Catch the appropriate exception or report it to the caller. Never print a success message unless the delete operation actually succeeded.

examples.title: Delete an existing file
examples.explanation: Files.delete removes the path, and exists confirms that it is no longer present.

examples.title: Delete only if present
examples.explanation: deleteIfExists returns false when the target path was absent.

examples.title: Delete an empty directory
examples.explanation: An empty directory can be deleted after it is created.

examples.title: Use File.delete result
examples.code:
import java.io.File;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { File file = new File("legacy.txt"); file.createNewFile(); System.out.println(file.delete()); } }
examples.explanation: File.delete returns true when the path was successfully deleted.

examples.title: Delete a file then confirm
examples.explanation: deleteIfExists reports that it removed the file, and the follow-up check confirms absence.

practise.guidedTask: Create a temporary file with Files.writeString, delete it with Files.deleteIfExists and print the returned boolean plus the final Files.exists result. Repeat the operation to demonstrate the false result for an already-absent path. Then create an empty directory and delete it.
practise.independentTask: Build a cleanup utility that deletes only a named temporary file inside a dedicated application test directory. Normalize the resolved path, verify that it remains under the approved base directory, use Files.deleteIfExists, and report success, absence and IOException separately. Test an existing file, a missing file and an empty directory.
hints: Use Files.delete when absence is an error and Files.deleteIfExists when absence is acceptable.
A non-empty directory cannot normally be removed with one Files.delete call.
Normalize and validate the target against a known application-owned base path, then handle IOException from the delete operation.
practise.challenge: Review a cleanup routine that accepts a user-provided path. Identify path traversal, symbolic-link and check-then-delete risks. Propose a safer design that restricts deletion to a dedicated directory and explain which race conditions still require care.

questions.prompt: Which method deletes a path and throws if deletion fails?
questions.explanation: delete() removes the target path and reports failure when it cannot delete it.

questions.prompt: What does deleteIfExists return for a missing path?
questions.explanation: The method returns false when the target already exists or creation did not occur.
The method's return value indicates whether deletion succeeded.

questions.prompt: Can a non-empty directory normally be deleted directly with Files.delete?
options: Yes, it always removes all children
questions.explanation: Deletion should not be assumed to succeed when the target is missing or cannot be removed.

questions.prompt: What should be done before a destructive delete operation?
questions.answer: Validate the target path and intended scope
options: Validate the target path and intended scope
questions.explanation: Validate the exact target before deletion to avoid removing unintended files.
